lead: A thin plate is a flat sheet whose thickness t is small compared with its width. Moments applied along its edges bend it, and the bending moment at any point depends only on how sharply the sheet is curved there. One number, the plate stiffness D = Et³/[12(1 − ν²)], links curvature to moment. This chapter builds that link from the Kirchhoff assumptions, adds the twisting moment, and shows when a bent plate becomes a saddle and when it becomes a dome.
prereq: You need: beam bending, σ = M y/I and M = EI/R, and Poisson's ratio.

blocks.text: A plate is thin when t is under about a tenth of its smaller span. Take x and y in the mid-surface and z upward from it, and let w(x, y) be the deflection.

The Kirchhoff assumptions: straight lines normal to the mid-surface stay straight and normal after bending; the mid-surface does not stretch; the deflection w is small compared with t; and the stress normal to the plate, σ<sub>z</sub>, is negligible. A point at height z then moves in the plane by u = −z ∂w/∂x and v = −z ∂w/∂y. Differentiating gives the strains:

blocks.where: ε<sub>x</sub>, ε<sub>y</sub> are direct strains and γ<sub>xy</sub> the engineering shear strain (dimensionless); z is the height above the mid-surface (m); w is the deflection (m).

blocks.text: Strain is zero at the mid-surface and largest at the faces. Define the curvatures so that a sagging plate has positive curvature:

blocks.where: κ<sub>x</sub> and κ<sub>y</sub> are the bending curvatures in the x and y directions and κ<sub>xy</sub> is the twist of the surface, all in m⁻¹. The shear strain is γ<sub>xy</sub> = 2zκ<sub>xy</sub>; the factor 2 belongs to the strain, not to the twist.

sections.h3: Moments and the plate stiffness D

blocks.text: With σ<sub>z</sub> = 0 each layer is in plane stress, so σ<sub>x</sub> = E(ε<sub>x</sub> + νε<sub>y</sub>)/(1 − ν²), σ<sub>y</sub> = E(ε<sub>y</sub> + νε<sub>x</sub>)/(1 − ν²) and τ<sub>xy</sub> = Gγ<sub>xy</sub> with G = E/2(1 + ν). A moment per unit width is stress times lever arm summed through the thickness, M<sub>x</sub> = ∫σ<sub>x</sub> z dz from −t/2 to t/2. Since ∫z² dz = t³/12, this gives:
M<sub>x</sub> = D(κ<sub>x</sub> + νκ<sub>y</sub>),   M<sub>y</sub> = D(κ<sub>y</sub> + νκ<sub>x</sub>),   M<sub>xy</sub> = D(1 − ν)κ<sub>xy</sub>
blocks.where: M<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>y</sub> are bending moments and M<sub>xy</sub> the twisting moment, each per unit length of edge, in N·m/m (that is, N); κ in m⁻¹; ν is Poisson's ratio.
D is the plate stiffness, or flexural rigidity (N·m); E is Young's modulus (Pa); t is the thickness (m).

blocks.text: The twisting moment is ∫τ<sub>xy</sub> z dz = 2G(t³/12)κ<sub>xy</sub> = D(1 − ν)κ<sub>xy</sub>. Some books give M<sub>xy</sub> the opposite sign; its size is the same.

Where does 1/(1 − ν²) come from? In cylindrical bending the plate cannot curve in y, so a lateral stress σ<sub>y</sub> = νσ<sub>x</sub> builds up, and each layer behaves as if its modulus were E/(1 − ν²) instead of E. A beam strip of unit width has EI = Et³/12, so a plate held flat across is stiffer by 1/(1 − ν²), about 1.10 for ν = 0.30. If the plate is free to curve in y the two effects cancel and M<sub>x</sub> = Et³κ<sub>x</sub>/12, the beam value.

The stress at the faces follows from the moment just as for a rectangular beam of unit width: σ<sub>x,max</sub> = 6M<sub>x</sub>/t² and σ<sub>y,max</sub> = 6M<sub>y</sub>/t², tension on the convex face.

Apply M<sub>x</sub> alone with the edges in y free, so M<sub>y</sub> = 0. Then κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub>: the sheet sags in x and hogs in y, a saddle. This is anticlastic bending. When the two principal curvatures have the same sign the surface is synclastic, like a dome or the centre of a plate under uniform pressure. Cylindrical bending is the case w = w(x) only: κ<sub>y</sub> = 0, and then M<sub>y</sub> = νM<sub>x</sub>, not zero.
Like a stress element, a plate under M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub> and M<sub>xy</sub> has two perpendicular directions with no twisting moment, on which the bending moments are largest and smallest:
M<sub>1,2</sub> = (M<sub>x</sub> + M<sub>y</sub>)/2 ± √[((M<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + M<sub>xy</sub>²],   tan 2α = 2M<sub>xy</sub>/(M<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>)
blocks.where: M<sub>1</sub> and M<sub>2</sub> are the principal moments (N·m/m); α is the angle from x to the direction of M<sub>1</sub>.

blocks.text: Pure twist, M<sub>xy</sub> = T alone, gives principal moments ±T at 45°: a saddle. Whether a surface is anticlastic or synclastic is decided by the signs of the principal curvatures, not of the moments. With both moments positive, the curvature κ<sub>2</sub> = (M<sub>2</sub> − νM<sub>1</sub>)/[D(1 − ν²)] is still negative when M<sub>2</sub> < νM<sub>1</sub>, and the plate is a saddle.

examples.question: A flat aluminium alloy plate 3 mm thick has E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.30. It is bent by edge moments M<sub>x</sub> with the plate free to curve in y, and its curvature in x is κ<sub>x</sub> = 0.05 m⁻¹. Find D, M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub> and the largest bending stress. Then repeat for cylindrical bending, κ<sub>y</sub> = 0, at the same κ<sub>x</sub>.
steps: Free in y: M<sub>y</sub> = 0 needs κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub> = −0.30 × 0.05 = −0.015 m⁻¹.
M<sub>x</sub> = D(κ<sub>x</sub> + νκ<sub>y</sub>) = 173.1 × (0.05 − 0.0045) = 173.1 × 0.0455 = 7.88 N·m/m. Check: Et³κ<sub>x</sub>/12 = 1890 × 0.05/12 = 7.88 N·m/m, the beam-strip value.
M<sub>y</sub> = D(κ<sub>y</sub> + νκ<sub>x</sub>) = 0, as the free edges require. Face stress: σ<sub>max</sub> = 6M<sub>x</sub>/t² = 6 × 7.88/(9 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.25 MPa.

Cylindrical bending: κ<sub>y</sub> = 0, so M<sub>x</sub> = Dκ<sub>x</sub> = 173.1 × 0.05 = 8.65 N·m/m and M<sub>y</sub> = νM<sub>x</sub> = 2.60 N·m/m. Face stress σ<sub>x</sub> = 5.77 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = νσ<sub>x</sub> = 1.73 MPa.
examples.answer: D = 173.1 N·m. Free in y: M<sub>x</sub> = 7.88 N·m/m, M<sub>y</sub> = 0, σ<sub>max</sub> = 5.25 MPa. Cylindrical: M<sub>x</sub> = 8.65 N·m/m, M<sub>y</sub> = 2.60 N·m/m, σ<sub>max</sub> = 5.77 MPa.

examples.question: The same 3 mm plate (D = 173.1 N·m) carries M<sub>x</sub> = 10 N·m/m, M<sub>y</sub> = 4 N·m/m and M<sub>xy</sub> = 4 N·m/m at a point. Find the principal moments and their direction, the largest bending stress, and the principal curvatures. Is the surface there synclastic or anticlastic?
steps: Centre and radius: (M<sub>x</sub> + M<sub>y</sub>)/2 = 7 N·m/m; √[((10 − 4)/2)² + 4²] = √(9 + 16) = 5 N·m/m.
Principal moments: M<sub>1</sub> = 7 + 5 = 12 N·m/m, M<sub>2</sub> = 7 − 5 = 2 N·m/m.
Direction: tan 2α = 2 × 4/(10 − 4) = 1.333, 2α = 53.13°, α = 26.57° from x to M<sub>1</sub>.
Largest stress: σ = 6M<sub>1</sub>/t² = 6 × 12/(9 × 10⁻⁶) = 8.00 MPa on the faces.

Shape: κ<sub>1</sub> and κ<sub>2</sub> have opposite signs, so the surface is anticlastic, even though both principal moments are positive, because M<sub>2</sub> = 2 is less than νM<sub>1</sub> = 3.6.
examples.answer: M<sub>1</sub> = 12 N·m/m at 26.6° to x, M<sub>2</sub> = 2 N·m/m; σ<sub>max</sub> = 8.0 MPa; κ<sub>1</sub> = 0.0724 m⁻¹, κ<sub>2</sub> = −0.0102 m⁻¹, so the surface is anticlastic.

traps: Using the beam value Et³/12 for D. D carries 1/(1 − ν²); dropping it makes a plate held flat across about 10% too flexible.
Mixing the two edge cases: free anticlastic bending has κ<sub>y</sub> = −νκ<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>y</sub> = 0; cylindrical bending has κ<sub>y</sub> = 0 and M<sub>y</sub> = νM<sub>x</sub>.

Putting a factor 2 into the twisting moment. The shear strain is γ<sub>xy</sub> = −2z ∂²w/∂x∂y, but M<sub>xy</sub> = D(1 − ν)κ<sub>xy</sub> with κ<sub>xy</sub> = −∂²w/∂x∂y; the 2 is absorbed in D(1 − ν) = 2G t³/12.
Judging saddle or dome from the signs of the moments. The shape follows the principal curvatures; two positive moments still give a saddle when M<sub>2</sub> < νM<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: State the Kirchhoff assumptions for a thin plate in bending.
quiz.a: Normals to the mid-surface stay straight and normal; the mid-surface does not stretch; the deflection is small compared with t; the normal stress σ<sub>z</sub> is negligible.

quiz.q: Why is a plate in cylindrical bending stiffer than a beam strip of the same width?
quiz.a: The plate cannot curve across, so a lateral stress νσ<sub>x</sub> builds up and each layer acts with modulus E/(1 − ν²). The moment for a given curvature rises by 1/(1 − ν²), about 10% for ν = 0.3.

quiz.q: Write the plate stiffness D and give its unit.
A 2 mm aluminium alloy plate, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, is bent with κ<sub>x</sub> = 0.02 m⁻¹ and is free in y. Find D and M<sub>x</sub>.
For the same κ<sub>x</sub>, which gives the larger M<sub>x</sub>: cylindrical bending or bending with free edges in y? By how much, for ν = 0.3?
quiz.a: Cylindrical bending: M<sub>x</sub> = Dκ<sub>x</sub>, against Dκ<sub>x</sub>(1 − ν²) when free. The ratio is 1/0.91 = 1.099, about 10% larger, because the restraint in y adds the Poisson term νκ<sub>y</sub> with no cancelling curvature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Thick plates and sandwich panels need transverse shear (Mindlin theory). Search for Kirchhoff–Love plate theory.
